SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
1
SE4030 | SECURE SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT
ICare Optical Store
Management System
Security Assessment Report
Application security findings, remediation review and verification requirements
Assessment date
16 October 2026
Environment
http://127.0.0.1:4010 - isolated local deployment
Assessment tool
OWASP ZAP 2.17.0
Test data
Synthetic users, orders, prescriptions and payment records
Coverage
Order processing, payment handling, password recovery, prescriptions
and support tickets
Executive overview
The assessment identified weaknesses in how ICare checks access to individual records,
validates payment information and handles password recovery. Ordinary customer
accounts could access or modify records belonging to other users. The order workflow also
accepted client-supplied prices and allowed an order to be marked as paid without
payment-provider evidence.
The ZAP report contains 11 High, 5 Medium, 4 Low and 1 Informational alert categories.
These totals include manually verified application findings and automatic passive alerts.
The automatic card-data alert and the manual card-data finding describe the same
underlying exposure, so alert totals should not be interpreted as counts of independent
defects.
The highest priorities are to enforce record ownership and staff permissions, calculate
prices on the server, remove sensitive card storage, and separate password-reset credentials
from API access credentials. Earlier remediation work is recorded where available; closure
requires repeat testing of the updated application.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
2
1. Scope and assessment method
1.1 Application areas
Testing covered authenticated order retrieval, order creation, payment and delivery
updates, prescription access, ticket responses, card-detail storage, account registration and
password reset. Public pages were also examined for security headers and externally loaded
resources. The target was the local application rather than a public production service.
1.2 Evidence collection
Manual tests used crafted HTTP requests sent through the ZAP proxy. Each recorded
finding has a VIVA identifier and a ZAP History marker. Alice and Bob represent separate
synthetic customer accounts. Requests using one account against the other account's
records were used to examine ownership checks. Anonymous and administrator requests
provide useful control cases where recorded.
Passive alerts were generated from traffic observed by ZAP. A passive alert can identify
exposed data or missing response protections, but does not by itself demonstrate a complete
attack. The report records 13 manual findings, including the Low-severity database error
disclosure. Twelve High- and Medium-severity manual findings form the member
allocation in this report.
1.3 Boundaries
No unrestricted active scan or production test was performed. The /api/seed endpoint,
external services and password-reset email delivery were excluded. Password-reset tests
used a synthetic server-compatible token fixture; they demonstrate token-processing
behavior rather than successful delivery or interception of a real reset email. Google sign-in
was outside the ZAP assessment.
1.4 Interpretation of remediation status
The earlier assessment describes code changes and mocked regression outcomes. Those
records provide a remediation history, while the ZAP assessment documents the vulnerable
behaviors observed in its test environment. A post-fix pass is established only by applying
the same scenario to the updated build and recording the result. The two attached PDFs do
not establish closure of all findings.
1.5 Severity basis
High findings affect confidentiality, payment integrity or account security. Medium
findings cover ticket misuse, weak passwords and missing browser protections. Low
findings concern error disclosure and response hardening. The Informational classification
is not a vulnerability.

This allocation identifies responsibility for reporting and remediation review. Individual
implementation authorship is established through repository history and project
contribution records.
2.1 Shared control requirements
Several findings arise from inconsistent authorization across related routes. A valid login
establishes who sent a request; the route must still decide whether that person may read the
selected object or perform the requested action. Read and write endpoints should apply the
same ownership rules, with additional role checks for privileged changes.
Payment controls require both authorization and trustworthy transaction evidence.
Restricting a route to an allowed account does not prove that money was collected.
Similarly, calculating a correct total does not protect a payment-update route that accepts
unsupported payment claims. Each control must be verified separately.
2.2 Evidence traceability
The finding sections retain the original VIVA identifiers, endpoint patterns and History
markers so that the documented behavior can be matched to the ZAP evidence. Source-file
locations refer to the assessed baseline and may move when code is revised.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
4
3. Order access and fulfilment
VIVA-01 | Cross-user order disclosure
Severity: High
Endpoint: GET /api/orders/:id
ZAP History: viva-0005
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/orderRoutes.js:107
Observed behavior
Alice used her bearer token to retrieve Bob's synthetic order and shipping address. An
anonymous control request returned 401. [1]
Security impact
An authenticated customer could obtain another customer's order and delivery information
if the order identifier were known. The anonymous rejection shows that login was required,
but the successful cross-user request shows that record ownership was not enforced.
Remediation approach
Load the order and compare its owner with the authenticated user before returning any
fields. Allow administrator access only where required by the staff workflow. Return a
consistent 403 or non-disclosing 404 for unrelated users.
Verification criteria
Repeat the request as the owner, another customer and an administrator. The owner should
retain access, the unrelated customer should receive no order data, and staff access should
match the approved policy. Also check list routes for the same exposure.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report records ownership checks and mocked results of owner=200 and
other-user=404. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
5
VIVA-04 | Cross-user payment-status modification
Severity: High
Endpoint: PUT /api/orders/:id/pay
ZAP History: viva-0010
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/orderRoutes.js:142
Observed behavior
Alice marked a separate order belonging to Bob as paid. This test examined ownership
independently of the payment-provider verification issue. [1]
Security impact
A customer could alter the financial status of another customer's order. Fulfilment
decisions or financial reports that trust this flag could then use an incorrect payment state.
Remediation approach
Restrict payment transitions to the supported payment workflow. A customer request must
not directly control another order's paid flag. For Cash on Delivery, allow only authorized
staff to record an actual collection; for a gateway, accept validated provider evidence
mapped to the correct order.
Verification criteria
Use another customer's token against the target order and confirm rejection with no state
change. Exercise the legitimate collection or gateway path separately, then repeat the same
event to confirm it cannot create duplicate payment records.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report describes an administrator-only route for recording Cash on Delivery
collections. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
6
VIVA-02 | Unauthorized delivery-state modification
Severity: High
Endpoint: PUT /api/orders/:id/deliver
ZAP History: viva-0006
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/orderRoutes.js:121
Observed behavior
An ordinary non-administrator changed Bob's isDelivered value from false to true. [1]
Security impact
A customer could falsely complete another user's delivery workflow. This could distort
order tracking, interfere with staff handling and create disputes about whether goods were
delivered.
Remediation approach
Require the authorized fulfilment role on the server before changing delivery state.
Validate the transition against the order workflow and record the actor, time, order and
previous state in an audit record.
Verification criteria
Confirm that anonymous and ordinary customer requests cannot change delivery status,
including requests against their own orders. Verify that an authorized staff action succeeds
and records the transition without modifying unrelated fields.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report states that delivery updates were changed to require administrator access.
[2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
7
4. Pricing and payment security
VIVA-05 | Client-controlled order price and total
Severity: High
Endpoint: POST /api/orders
ZAP History: viva-0011
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/orderRoutes.js:26
Observed behavior
The fixture catalog listed a product at 100, but a request containing a price and total of 0.01
created an order using the submitted values. [1]
Security impact
A customer could reduce the recorded amount payable by editing the request. A correct
total displayed in the browser offers no protection when the API trusts client-controlled
pricing.
Remediation approach
Accept product identifiers and validated quantities, then retrieve current prices from the
server-side catalog. Recalculate item totals, shipping, tax and the final amount on the
server. Validate stock and reject invalid quantities or unsupported payment methods.
Verification criteria
Submit a valid product with a forged price and total. The server should either reject the
inconsistent request or create the order at its own calculated amount. Include negative,
zero, fractional and excessive quantities according to the product rules.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report describes catalog-price lookup, server-side recalculation and a mocked
tampering regression test. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
8
VIVA-09 | Sensitive payment-card storage and exposure
Severity: High
Endpoint: GET /api/card-details
ZAP History: viva-0018
Baseline source: ICare/backend/models/cardModel.js:7; routes/cardRoutes.js:35
Observed behavior
A subsequent GET returned the complete synthetic test card number and CVV. The
recorded source review found ordinary string persistence without field encryption. [1]
Security impact
Disclosure extends beyond the initial submission because stored values remain retrievable.
An exposed database, API response or diagnostic log could reveal sensitive payment
information. The passive PII alert supports the same exposure rather than a separate
independent defect.
Remediation approach
Remove CVV persistence and exclude sensitive card fields from every response. Prefer a
hosted payment-provider flow that returns a token and only the metadata needed by the
application. If online payment is unavailable, disable that path. Address historical records,
logs and backups through a controlled removal process.
Verification criteria
Check that retired card routes cannot read or write sensitive values and that checkout no
longer submits them. Inspect database records and relevant logs for residual data. If a
gateway is introduced, confirm that only permitted tokens and masked metadata are
retained.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report describes removal of the card form, API and data fields, with checkout
limited to Cash on Delivery. Historical data removal remained outstanding. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
9
VIVA-03 | Paid status without provider verification
Severity: High
Endpoint: PUT /api/orders/:id/pay
ZAP History: viva-0009
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/orderRoutes.js:137
Observed behavior
An empty JSON request marked an unpaid PayPal order as paid without capture proof.
External integrations were disabled during the assessment. [1]
Security impact
The application could record a successful payment without evidence that a transaction
occurred. An attacker would not need to defeat the payment provider if the application
accepts its own unverified status update.
Remediation approach
For gateway payments, verify transaction status through a trusted server-to-server process
and match the transaction to the order, amount and currency. Reject replayed or unrelated
transaction references. Until a verified integration is available, disable unsupported online
payment methods and retain only the supported collection workflow.
Verification criteria
Attempt a payment update with an empty body, fabricated transaction reference, incorrect
amount and wrong order mapping. None should mark the order paid. Test the legitimate
supported payment path and confirm that repeated processing is safe.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report states that unsupported card payments were removed and staff could
record only collected Cash on Delivery payments. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
10
5. Account and password recovery
VIVA-10 | Password-reset token reuse
Severity: High
Endpoint: POST /api/users/reset-password
ZAP History: viva-0020
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/userRoutes.js:107
Observed behavior
The same server-compatible fixture token changed the password twice. Login confirmed
the second password. The token was seeded directly to avoid sending reset email. [1]
Security impact
A reset credential remained usable after completing its intended action. Someone who
retained a usable token could change the password again during its validity period,
undermining account recovery.
Remediation approach
Issue a short-lived, high-entropy one-time reset token, store its hash and associate it with
the intended account. Check expiry and consume the token atomically with the password
change. Apply session revocation according to the account-recovery policy.
Verification criteria
Use a valid token once and confirm successful login with the new password. Reuse the
token and confirm rejection without a further password change. Test expired tokens and
concurrent submissions to verify that at most one reset succeeds.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report describes a hashed one-time token with a 15-minute lifetime and atomic
consumption. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
11
VIVA-11 | Reset token accepted as an API access token
Severity: High
Endpoint: GET /api/card-details
ZAP History: viva-0022
Baseline source: ICare/backend/utils.js:27; routes/userRoutes.js:73
Observed behavior
A JWT generated with the application's reset signing logic and containing the reset-flow
user ID was accepted as a bearer token. The protected endpoint returned the synthetic card
record. [1]
Security impact
A credential intended only for password recovery could be used for authenticated API
access. This expands the authority of a reset token beyond its intended purpose and
weakens separation between authentication flows.
Remediation approach
Use distinct reset and access-token validation paths. Access middleware should require the
expected token purpose, issuer, audience, expiry and algorithm. A random reset token
stored by hash avoids treating a reset credential as a general access JWT.
Verification criteria
Present a reset credential to protected endpoints and require rejection before any data is
returned. Confirm that a valid access token still works. If card routes have been removed,
also test an existing protected endpoint so that route removal does not conceal a
token-validation defect.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report discusses revised reset tokens but provides no explicit post-fix test of
reset-token rejection by API access middleware. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
12
VIVA-12 | Single-character registration password
Severity: Medium
Endpoint: POST /api/users/signup
ZAP History: viva-0023
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/userRoutes.js:197
Observed behavior
A direct API signup request using the password a succeeded and issued a token, bypassing
browser-only validation. [1]
Security impact
Accounts could be created with extremely easy-to-guess passwords. Browser restrictions
do not protect the API because requests can be submitted without using the application
form.
Remediation approach
Apply a documented password-length policy in the backend for registration and password
changes, including recovery. Reject known-compromised passwords where supported and
provide clear validation feedback. Keep browser validation consistent with the server
policy.
Verification criteria
Submit the original single-character password directly to the API and confirm rejection
without account creation or token issuance. Test boundary lengths, the recovery path and a
valid passphrase to ensure enforcement is consistent.
Recorded remediation status
Neither attached report establishes a completed remediation for this finding. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
13
6. Prescription and support security
VIVA-06 | Prescription disclosure to an unrelated customer
Severity: High
Endpoint: GET /api/prescriptions/:id
ZAP History: viva-0012
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/prescriptionRoutes.js:41
Observed behavior
Alice read the synthetic Bob Demo prescription using an ordinary customer token. [1]
Security impact
An unrelated customer could access another patient's prescription information. Possession
of a record identifier should not grant access to clinical or patient-specific data.
Remediation approach
Associate each prescription with the correct patient and apply the approved read policy on
the server. Permit access only to the patient where supported and to authorized staff. Limit
returned fields to those required for the permitted task.
Verification criteria
Request a prescription as the intended patient, an unrelated customer and authorized staff.
Confirm that only roles permitted by the application policy receive data. Include listing and
search routes so that the same record cannot be exposed indirectly.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report describes administrator-only prescription management and mocked
results of customer=403 and admin=200. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
14
VIVA-07 | Unauthorized prescription modification
Severity: High
Endpoint: PUT /api/prescriptions/:id
ZAP History: viva-0013
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/prescriptionRoutes.js:55
Observed behavior
Alice changed another patient's synthetic prescription without a clinician or administrator
role. [1]
Security impact
Unauthorized edits could undermine the accuracy of information used to prepare an optical
order. This affects record integrity as well as patient confidentiality.
Remediation approach
Restrict writes to staff authorized to manage prescriptions and validate access to the
selected patient record. Allowlist editable fields, validate clinical data types and ranges
against application rules, and record changes for traceability.
Verification criteria
Attempt the update as an unrelated customer and verify both rejection and unchanged
stored values. Test a legitimate staff update, invalid fields and attempts to change
ownership. Review the audit record for actor, time and modified fields.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report states that administrator checks were added to prescription-management
routes. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
15
VIVA-08 | Cross-user support-ticket response injection
Severity: Medium
Endpoint: POST /api/tickets/:id/responses
ZAP History: viva-0015
Baseline source: ICare/backend/routes/ticketRoutes.js:122
Observed behavior
Alice received 404 when reading Bob's ticket, but appended a response with a 201 result.
The inserted response was confirmed using Bob's token. [1]
Security impact
A customer could interfere with another customer's support conversation despite being
unable to read it. Unauthorized messages could mislead the customer or staff and reduce
trust in the support history.
Remediation approach
Apply the same owner-or-authorized-staff check to response creation as to ticket retrieval.
Resolve response authorship from the authenticated session and prevent client input from
assigning another author or staff identity.
Verification criteria
Confirm that an unrelated customer cannot append a response and that the response list
remains unchanged. Verify that the ticket owner and permitted staff can respond, with the
correct server-derived author and role.
Recorded remediation status
The earlier report describes owner-or-administrator response authorization and a mocked
other-user=404 regression result. [2]
Post-fix closure requires a recorded retest against the updated build.

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
16
7. Additional security observations
7.1 Browser response protections
The assessed pages lacked Content-Security-Policy and anti-clickjacking protections.
Define a policy using the resources the application actually needs and configure
frame-ancestors to restrict embedding. Where appropriate, X-Frame-Options can provide
additional compatibility. Test the policy against checkout and sign-in pages before
enforcing it broadly. Missing headers reduce defensive coverage; these observations do not
establish that an XSS or clickjacking exploit was executed. [1]
The external Font Awesome stylesheet had no integrity attribute. Pin the resource version
and use a matching integrity hash with the required cross-origin setting, or serve the
reviewed asset locally. Verify that the stylesheet loads correctly and that an altered resource
is rejected when integrity protection is used. [1]
7.2 Error handling and disclosure
A malformed order identifier produced HTTP 500, and manual finding VIVA-13 recorded
internal database cast details in an error response. These observations overlap in the
error-handling area. Validate identifier syntax before querying the database and return a
controlled client error. Central error handling should keep stack traces, database details and
internal paths out of responses while retaining useful server-side diagnostics. [1]
7.3 Other response headers
The application exposed the Express framework through X-Powered-By and omitted
X-Content-Type-Options. Disable unnecessary framework identification and set nosniff
alongside correct content types. Recheck successful responses, authentication failures and
error pages because middleware coverage may differ between response paths. [1]
7.4 Alert counting
The automatic PII Disclosure alert includes two card-detail instances. It corroborates
VIVA-09 and is not an additional independent payment defect. The Modern Web
Application alert is Informational and does not require vulnerability closure. The scanner's
zero false-positive field is report metadata, rather than an independent validation of every
alert. [1]

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
17
8. Google OpenID Connect
The earlier ICare assessment records a Sign in with Google feature under Kojithan's
additional contribution. Its described design uses the authorization-code flow with the
openid, email and profile scopes. Google sign-in was excluded from the ZAP assessment,
so its functional and security results are considered separately. [2]
8.1 Recorded design
The design described in the earlier report uses state to bind the callback to the initiated
login, nonce to bind the ID token to that flow, and a PKCE verifier to bind code exchange
to the initiating client. Short-lived HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Lax hold flow-related
values. The backend validates the Google ID-token signature and claims before resolving
the account. [2]
Google accounts are resolved using the provider subject identifier, sub. New users receive
non-administrator accounts, and an email match alone does not automatically link a Google
identity to an existing password account. These choices help preserve the distinction
between account identification and authorized account linking. [2]
8.2 Recorded testing and configuration
The earlier assessment records a dedicated Google Cloud testing client, a localhost backend
redirect URI and a consent/sign-in test on 25 September 2026. It also describes
token-validation tests and configuration stored in an ignored backend .env file. These are
historical implementation records rather than results from the 16 October ZAP assessment.
[2]
8.3 Verification requirements
Repeat sign-in with the configured redirect URI and confirm creation or selection of the
expected non-administrator account. Reject missing or mismatched state and nonce, invalid
or expired ID tokens, and inappropriate issuer or audience claims. Check that flow cookies
expire or are cleared after completion and that replayed callbacks cannot establish a fresh
session.
For existing local accounts, test the account-linking policy explicitly. Verify that a
matching email does not silently replace the local authentication method. Keep OAuth
client credentials out of repository history and logs, and rotate any previously exposed
credentials.

9.1 Retest procedure
Use an isolated database with separate customer and staff accounts. Record the build or
commit tested and reset fixture state before each scenario. Replay each VIVA case through
ZAP, then inspect both the HTTP response and resulting stored state. A denied response
alone is insufficient if a write already occurred.
For each result, retain the finding identifier, test date, role, request, response, expected
outcome and observed database effect. Link remediation commits to the corresponding
finding. Use only synthetic credentials and records in retained evidence. Include successful
legitimate operations to confirm that the control has not broken the intended workflow.
9.2 Outstanding operational work
The earlier assessment identifies historical .env secrets and retained card records as
follow-up work. Credential rotation and removal of historical sensitive data require checks
beyond route-level fixes. Dependency review, rate limiting, browser token storage and live
integration testing also remain separate review activities; they are not demonstrated as
resolved by the supplied ZAP scan. [2]

SE4030 | ICare Security Assessment
19
10. Assessment conclusion
ICare's main security weaknesses occur at the API boundary. The recorded tests show that
authentication alone did not prevent access to another customer's records, and that
client-controlled values influenced financial and fulfilment decisions. Password-recovery
credentials also lacked the restrictions needed for a one-time, purpose-specific action.
The remediation work described in the earlier assessment addresses several of these areas
through ownership checks, staff restrictions, server-side totals, Cash on Delivery checkout
and revised reset tokens. The remaining task is to demonstrate those controls on the
updated application using repeatable tests. Findings should be closed only when the
original misuse is blocked and the legitimate workflow continues to function.
The final security position therefore depends on both application fixes and operational
follow-through: residual card data must be addressed, exposed secrets rotated, and
supported authentication and payment flows tested in their intended configuration. The
ZAP History identifiers in this report provide the link between each documented weakness
and its verification scenario.
11. Evidence sources
[1] Optical Store Management System - ZAP Security Assessment. OWASP ZAP 2.17.0, generated 16
October 2026. Attached file: optical-store-zap-report(2).pdf. Primary evidence for alert counts, manual
findings, endpoint details and assessment exclusions.
[2] ICare Optical Store Management System - Revised Security Assessment Report. Attached file:
SE4030_ICare_ZAP_Based_Revised_Report(1).pdf. Source for member allocation, recorded earlier
implementation work and Google OpenID Connect design. Its descriptions of the 25 September
assessment are used as historical records; that original assessment was not separately attached.
11.1 Evidence coverage
This report is based on the two attached PDFs. It does not add new scan results, repository inspections or
live payment-provider tests. Remediation approaches and verification criteria describe the controls to
implement or confirm; they are not presented as completed test outcomes.

Scope and reproducibility
Method
Isolated synthetic database; authenticated manual regression requests through actual ZAP proxy plus passive
scanning of visited HTML, assets, and API responses. No unrestricted active scan, external service testing,
Google login, or password-reset email delivery. Reset fixture seeded directly. No real customer data used.
Coverage
Home, sign-in, sign-up, manifest, robots, production JavaScript/CSS assets, card endpoint removal, server-side
pricing, order ownership, payment and delivery authorization, reset replay, session revocation, reset/access
JWT separation, prescription authorization, ticket ownership, weak registration passwords, malformed
identifiers, and response headers. Positive owner/admin controls were included.
Limits and remaining work
This is a targeted authenticated regression assessment plus passive scan, not an unrestricted active scan.
Google consent, Cloudinary, email delivery, external payment services and deployment TLS were not
exercised. Production headers were tested using NODE_ENV=production on local HTTP; this does not verify
real HTTPS configuration. External CDN resources were not actively scanned. Business rules not listed above
and dependency vulnerabilities require separate assessment.
The CSP deliberately allows inline styles needed by the current React/Bootstrap UI and selected Google
resources. A scanner may flag this as a hardening opportunity even though the original missing-CSP finding is
resolved. Review every fresh passive alert before claiming a zero-alert scan.
The configured existing application database was separately checked read-only on 16 October 2026: zero
legacy cards documents and zero orders with cardDetails. The isolated retest database does not establish the
state of other deployments or backups. The browser cleanup runs when the upgraded app is opened.
